newsitem.title: USA: Dole campaign enters last lap harried, no schedule.
newsitem.headline: Dole campaign enters last lap harried, no schedule.

text.p: Republican candidate Bob Dole entered the final stretch of his underdog campaign for president on Tuesday literally trying to figure out where he was going.

Lagging behind President Bill Clinton with only a week left until the election, Dole's campaign -- which until now has exhibited few signs of frenzy -- was beginning to show last-minute wear and tear.
Aides scrambled to work out a travel schedule for the final days which changed from hour to hour and was likely to become even less predictable as the election loomed.

The candidate himself seemed a little discombobulated in a speech to the World Affairs Council of Orange County on Tuesday morning as he wrapped up a four-day campaign swing in the crucial state of California.
While digging into Clinton as weak on foreign policy, Dole admitted, "as everybody here knows, not many voters consider foreign policy when they walk into the voting booth."
Until late on Monday the campaign did not know where Dole would be spending Tuesday. Dole's schedule for Wednesday is tentatively set, but up in the air beyond that point.

"We're a lean, aggressive campaign. We're mobile, we go where we need to go," said Dole press secretary Nelson Warfield, saying Dole was consulting with his campaign manager and evaluating polling data as he tried to determine where to spend his final days on the road.

Polls show Dole lagging Clinton by double-digit margins nationwide and in California, with time running out fast. The fact that Dole felt compelled to campaign in Orange County, usually a Republican stronghold, at this late date is a telling sign of the troubles he faces.
No Republican presidential candidate has lost Orange County since 1936, but polls show Dole only slightly ahead of Clinton here.

Campaign strategists claim their internal polls show Dole within single digits of Clinton in this must-win state, which has 54 of the 270 electoral college votes needed to win the White House. But a Los Angeles Times poll last week showed him trailing by 20 points.
In Denver, Dole reiterated his support for a controversial ballot measure giving parents more rights to challenge government decisions.
Earlier in Irvine, Dole again ran through a litany of White House scandals, trying to make the case that Clinton did not have the character to be re-elected.
"You're electing a president, not a talk-show host," Dole said, warning voters not to be fooled by Clinton's warm and fuzzy persona.
Describing Clinton's plan for an education tax credit, he said sarcastically, "You've got to go to college. You've got to get a 'B' average. You've got to keep your room clean."
He added, "Maybe Craig Livingstone will be the room cleaner," referring to a White House security aide removed for improperly requesting Republican FBI files.

Dole also continued to slam The New York Times, which he has called an arm of the Democratic National Committee after the newspaper endorsed Clinton. Describing his support for the 10th Amendment to the U.S. constitution, Dole said it was 28 words long, "That's about what I will get in The New York Times today. They'll all be negative."
The Times on Tuesday had a front page story on Dole's Monday speech in San Diego on affirmative action that was considerably longer than 28 words.
